extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, historians of mathematics, and mathematicians interested in mathematical practice
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative criteria and desiderata for a philosophy of mathematics that is faithful to mathematical practice, including standards for explanation, visualization, purity, axiomatic choice, and the treatment of computer and physical arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy of 'real' mathematics (Corfield's criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Work should be informed by the concerns of mathematicians past and present rather than done on the basis of at best token contact with its history or practice (Corfield, 2003, p. 3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corfield proposes drawing a line between philosophizing that takes history and practice seriously and that which treats history as mere 'history'. He criticizes the 'foundationalist filter' that privileges 1880–1930 foundational debates and ignores most of real 20th century mathematics; the pars construens of his project consists in philosophical analyses of localized case studies from mainstream mathematics (e.g., interplay with computer science, n-dimensional algebras, algebraic topology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain importance/fruitfulness of mathematical entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for why some mathematical entities are important, natural, and fruitful while others are not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate objective features (not merely subjective taste) that explain judgments of importance, such as fruitfulness in unifying results or opening new vistas; see Corfield's motivating list and Tappenden on concepts and definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for connectivity of mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how concepts developed in one area of mathematics can unexpectedly connect to unrelated concepts in other areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study historical and practice-based examples showing cross-connections; analyze mechanisms (analogies, conceptual generalizations, structural unification) by which such connectivity arises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain limits of computer proofs for understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarify why computer proofs may be unable to provide the sort of understanding at which mathematicians aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish epistemic roles of computers (discovery, experimental confirmation, calculation, formal verification) and investigate which roles contribute to understanding versus mere correctness; consider formal verification's potential to assist accounts of mathematical understanding (Avigad).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of analogy and inductive reasoning (including Bayesianism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for the role of analogy and other types of inductive reasoning in mathematics and whether Bayesianism can be applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how analogical and inductive methods contribute to discovery, justification, and theory choice; examine limits and legitimate uses within mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship between diagrammatic thinking and formal reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how diagrammatic (visual/diagram-based) thinking relates to and can be reconciled with formal symbolic reasoning, and account for the fruitfulness of diagrammatic reasoning in areas like algebraic topology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate stability and epistemic legitimacy of diagrammatic systems (e.g., in geometry and knot theory), and investigate when diagrammatic reasoning provides genuine mathematical knowledge rather than mere heuristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithfulness to mathematical practice as a criterion of adequacy (Maddy)
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory philosophy of mathematics should be faithful to mathematical practice; if philosophy conflicts with successful mathematical practice, philosophy must give (Maddy, 1990; 1997).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical accounts should model justificatory structures actually used by mathematicians and avoid imposing external philosophical ideals that contradict practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological virtues for justifying new axioms (Maddy's list)
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating proposals for new axioms (e.g., in set theory), consider verifiable consequence; powerful new methods for solving pre-existing problems; simplifying and systematizing theories; implying previous conjectures; implying 'natural' results; strong intertheoretic connections; and providing new insights into old theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors function as aspects of extrinsic justification for axioms and should be articulated and weighed to help set-theorists make rational choices between competing axiom candidates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalized model of practice (Maddy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct a naturalized model that identifies the goals of a mathematical practice and evaluates the methodology employed in that branch of mathematics relative to those goals (purified of irrelevant philosophical material and amplified by precise analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The model should claim that excised material is irrelevant, that identified goals are actual goals of the practice, that the portrayed interaction of goals is accurate, and that the means-ends reasoning employed is sound; if the practice approximates this model, it is rational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory power as epistemic virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess proofs and presentations not merely for truth but for their explanatory power — whether they tell us why a result is true and provide understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that different proofs offer different epistemic virtues; alternative proofs are often sought for explanatory aims. Models of explanation (e.g., Kitcher’s unification) can be tested against case studies (Mancosu & Hafner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity of methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Value proofs that avoid appeal to 'ideal' elements (purity), and analyze epistemic gains from either seeking or eliminating such ideal elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (e.g., elementary proofs of the prime number theorem) show why purity is cherished. Proof theory offers conservativity results about elimination of ideal elements, but philosophical work must ask why purity is epistemically valuable in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fruitfulness and naturalness of concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge mathematical concepts by fruitfulness and naturalness: whether a concept provides a natural setting for development, unifies results, or opens new vistas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate whether judgments of naturalness have objective features that can be philosophically analyzed (e.g., Riemann’s conceptual approach and subsequent fruitfulness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess legitimacy and reliability of visual/diagrammatic thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine which kinds and uses of visual thinking are legitimate and what epistemic roles visualization can play in proof, discovery, and understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical tensions exist (Kantian endorsement vs. late 19th-century skepticism: 'proof independent of the figure'). Philosophers should clarify when visualization is merely heuristic and when it carries epistemic weight; consider cognitive grasp, stability of diagrammatic inference, and influence of computer imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterize mathematical evidence and understanding in the age of computation
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy must extend ordinary epistemology of mathematics to address issues raised by computers: what counts as mathematical evidence and how formal verification relates to understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computers provide discovery, experimental confirmation, calculation, and formal verification; philosophers should assess how each contributes to evidence and whether formal verification can enhance accounts of understanding (Avigad).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat non-rigorous but fruitful physical arguments seriously
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not dismiss non-rigorous arguments from mathematical physics simply because they lack full rigor; attempt to make sense of them and to bring physicists’ insights into rigorous argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize differing standards of acceptability between physics and pure mathematics; analyze examples of 'non-rigorous' proofs that have been fruitful (e.g., in low-dimensional topology) and explore paths to rigorous reformulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to structuralism and unification (Category theory perspective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for the structuralist practices in contemporary mathematics (as exemplified by category theory) and their unifying power when evaluating foundations or explanatory virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical accounts should pay attention to the 'structuralism embodied in the practice' (McLarty) as this can explain the unifying spirit and fruitfulness of structural methods; do not reduce these phenomena to set-theoretic reductionism without careful analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use localized case studies integrated with general philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine detailed, localized case studies drawn from diverse areas (geometry, complex analysis, algebraic geometry, category theory, computer science, mathematical physics) with general philosophical reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than proposing grand unified theories of mathematical growth, pursue a broad program of analytic investigations across many case studies and integrate their lessons with traditional ontological and epistemological topics.
